newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Euro defence industry on ropes, awaits k.o.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Euro defence industry on ropes, awaits k.o.

text.p: "When you share a flat with Mike Tyson, guess who does the washing-up?" lamented a European defence industrialist as he surveyed the size and power of the restructured United States defence industry.

With the European Commission about to give its verdict on the proposed merger of U.S. giants Boeing and McDonnell-Douglas, concern has grown the tie-up could deal the last blow to a tottering European defence industry.

European defence companies, whose own faltering attempts at cross-border cooperation have been hampered by regulation and ancient rivalries, say they simply cannot compete with the huge conglomerates now forming on the opposite side of the Atlantic.

"What is now at stake is is the very survival of any real European defence industry," said a senior defence procurement official at NATO's Brussels headquarters which has watched recent developments with increasing unease, bordering on alarm.
He said the Europeans were now years behind the Americans and could not catch up "even if they wanted to".
The Boeing-McDonnell merger, which would create a group with annual sales of $48 billion, follows the creation of the Godzilla Lockheed Martin group last year.
These two and a third giant, Loral Corp, now appear set to dominate the market, leaving "only crumbs to the Europeans".
NATO WORRIED ABOUT STRATEGIC IMPLICATIONS

"This year the revenue of Lockheed-Martin will be roughly the same as the entire procurement spending of Britain and France combined. When you get a disparity of that size it begins to worry people," the official added.

Experts at the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), the West's defence shield, have grown increasingly worried over the strategic implications of the transatlantic imblance and the danger European suppliers will now also be wiped out.

"Such mergers will allow commercial costing to be brought to military procurement, that currently spells disaster for the European industry," said one senior military commander, responsible for defence purchases.

At a conference in Brussels on the future of the European defence industry last week, several participants expressed frustration with European governments, particularly France, for dithering while the Americans raced ahead.

Sir Geoffrey Battie, chairman of GEC defence division GEC-Marconi, said he believed the battle for a viable alternative to the United States in defence had been lost and it was now a question of saving what one could of the European industry.
But he was pessimistic over whether the Europeans would be able to accept the consequences of the rationalisation needed.
"I do not believe the Euro-defence industry will come together in time before it is engulfed by the U.S.," he said.
DEALS WITH U.S. COMPANIES

Pattie and other European industrialists say frustration with Europe's failure to remove barriers to trans-national integration will force several European companies to save what they can by entering into deals with the major U.S. companies.
This, they say, lay behind British Aerospace's recent decision to team up with Lockheed Martin in a bid to build the U.S. Joint Strike Fighter -- an aircraft intended for all the U.S. armed forces.
Boeing has been competing for the contract to build 3,000 of the planes, each with a price tag of $30 million.

"As the rate of progress in Europe is so small, it makes sense for these companies to piggy back on to the U.S. giants, though of course in the long term that's more bad news for the European industry," added one independent defence analyst.
Critics say nothing points up the Europeans failure to address the problem more than the new French leftwing government's foot-dragging over the future of France's industry.

French Defence Minister Alain Richard has said he will not be rushed into decisions on allowing the merger of aircraft companies Dassault Aviation and Aerospatiale and the sell-off of defence electronics giant Thomson-CSF.
"France is already three or four behind the other Europeans, let alone the Americans," said one defence industry specialist.
NATO ENLARGEMENT TO HAVE MINIMAL IMPACT

NATO officials said hopes that the imminent enlargement of the alliance to take in former communist countries, such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, would open new markets for the Europeans were unlikely to be realised.

"Enlargement will have a minimal impact, basically because these countries have little money and have been told for political reasons they can hang on to their old gear for now and just upgrade it where possible," said one NATO diplomat.
Last year, Poland's entire defence budget totalled only $3.1 billion. Recent estimates for replacing the country's air communications system put the cost at $1.3 billion over 15 years.
"There is no pot of gold out east," added the diplomat. "And what there is the Americans are already in there sewing up with cut-price deals."
